title: Throughput econ sensitivity ladder: latency/cost/quality tolerance study
body:
Purpose:
This note captures the sensitivity-ladder experiment we ran to map the tradeoffs between latency, unit cost, and quality for candidate models during onboarding. The goal: produce an operational tolerance curve that the model-team, runtime, and product can use to pick default serving knobs (batch size, cache prefix policy, max_tokens cap) and set regression detection thresholds for future rollouts.

Background and motivation:
- We frequently see onboarding teams accept higher cost to preserve quality or lower latency by reducing max_tokens or enabling aggressive batching. There is no unified artifact that expresses how much quality we give up per microsecond saved and per cent of cost reduced.
- This experiment tries to quantify the marginal utility (quality delta per unit latency or cost) across the common axes we control in serving: batch size, prefix caching aggressiveness, and max_tokens caps.

Dataset and prompt stratification:
- Prompt set: 1.2k samples derived from the standard onboarding corpus but reweighted to emphasize long-form generations (400–1,200 tokens), multi-turn context (avg context length 6 turns), and instruction-following. We call this "stratified-long-1k".
- Quality metrics: ROUGE-L, BLEU (for deterministic tasks), and a pass/fail binary for a manual rubric on 150 gold examples (semantic correctness + hallucination). Also track perplexity where applicable.
- Latency measurement: p50/p90 end-to-end server-side generation time excluding client/network; token-level generation time for tail analysis.
- Cost proxy: measured GPU-seconds per request and normalized token cost using our internal cost model (tokens * kernel time factor).

Experiment matrix (sparse factorial):
- Batch size: [1, 4, 8, 16] (continuous sweep for critical ranges)
- Cache policy: [off, prefix-only (100 tokens), prefix-aggressive (300 tokens), kv-warmup]
- max_tokens cap for generation: [256, 512, 768, 1024]
- Two model variants tested: candidate-v1 (float16 baseline) and candidate-q8 (8-bit quantized variant with slightly degraded perplexity).
- We run 20 repeats per cell to estimate sampling variance.

Key operational knobs used during runs:
- Batching timeout: 10ms (we also did a 5ms sensitivity check)
- Prefetch warmup for kv-warmup: first 50 sequences warmed per GPU, asynchronous prefetching enabled
- Request routing: pinned to single GPU slice to avoid multi-host variance

Summary of results (high level):
- Latency vs batch size: p50 increases sublinearly with batch size, p90 shows steeper growth beyond batch=8. Batch=4 achieved ~1.8x throughput with p90 increase of 12% vs batch=1. Batch=16 increases p90 by ~55% on average for long-form prompts.
- Cost per request: batching lowers cost/unit up to batch=8, marginal improvements after that because max token generation dominates compute.
- Caching impact: prefix-only caching (100 tokens) reduced average latency by 18% and reduced cost by ~12% for multi-turn prompts; prefix-aggressive (300 tokens) added another ~6% improvement but caused quality regressions on 3% of the golden subset (stale prefix reuse affecting entity resolution).
- max_tokens cap: dropping cap from 1024 to 512 cut mean GPU-seconds/request by ~37% and median latency by ~28% but degraded pass-rate on the gold rubric by 11 points for long-form summarization tasks.
- Quantized model (candidate-q8): lowers cost per token by ~22% but increases hallucination rate on the gold rubric by 4 points; latency profile similar but slightly noisier on tail (p95/p99).

Marginal tradeoff curves (operational takeaways):
- If product requires <5% quality delta vs baseline: use batch=4, prefix-only cache(100), max_tokens=768, candidate-q8 acceptable only if connected with stricter hallucination post-filtering. This configuration yields ~30% cost savings with <3% quality loss and p90 latency within SLO for most traffic distributions.
- If SLO: p90 < 800ms for long-form: batch must be <=4 and max_tokens<=512; this yields >25% quality degradation on some summarization prompts — consider model-upgrade or fallback policy for summarization routes.
- For throughput-first (e.g., embeddings-derived rerank frontend): batch=8 + prefix-aggressive yields best cost curve but add a rerank verification step to catch prefix-induced inconsistencies.

Regression detection heuristics proposed:
- Delta-quality threshold: raise alert when gold-pass rate drops >5% over rolling 24h relative baseline for onboarding promptset (stratified-long-1k).
- Latency shift rule: p90 increases >20% for three consecutive windows (1h windows) -> auto-canary rollback to previous model variant.
- Cost spike rule: normalized cost per 1k tokens increases >15% without commensurate quality improvement (quality delta < 1%) -> flag for efficiency review.

Unexpected findings and notes:
- "Quality shocks" at high cache aggressiveness: 3% of cases showed brittle answers that repeated cached prefixes incorrectly; these were concentrated in prompts with local entity updates (e.g., "In our last message we changed X to Y"). We added a synthetic prompt subset to detect this class automatically.
- Batch-timeouts interact with prefetch: lowering batching timeout from 10ms to 5ms reduced p90 tail for small batches but slightly increased cost due to reduced packing efficiency — choose timeout based on traffic burstiness.
- Quantized variant shows more p99 variance under microbursts; SRE should instrument per-GPU queue depth differential to avoid spiky tails.

Draft canonical recommendations for onboarding checklist (short):
1) Run sensitivity-ladder on stratified-long-1k before approving defaults. Record curves for batch vs quality and max_tokens vs quality.
2) Default knobs for long-content routes: batch=4, cache=prefix-100, max_tokens=768, policy=canary(10%) over 24h.
3) If using quantized candidate, enable hallucination post-filter at <1% false-positive tolerance and extend canary to 48h for q8 variants.
4) Add synthetic "entity-update" prompt partition to onboarding promptset to detect cache-induced regressions early.

Planned follow-ups and TODOs:
- (Marcus) Add an automated generator that creates the stratified-long-1k with explicit entity-update cases (due 2025-09-12).
- (Sofia) Integrate the regression heuristics into the rollout job as alerting rules (ENG-9280, due 2025-09-18).
- (Diego) Run a cloud-region sensitivity sweep to confirm prefix-warmup benefits hold across AZs (start 2025-09-10).
- Produce a short one-pager for product summarization owners describing expected quality delta across SLO choices (deliverable 2025-09-15).

Appendix: detailed cell highlights (examples) – excerpted:
- batch=8, cache=off, max_tokens=1024, candidate-v1: pass-rate 78% (gold), p90 1.34s, cost 1.00x baseline.
- batch=4, cache=prefix-100, max_tokens=768, candidate-q8: pass-rate 74%, p90 1.12s, cost 0.68x baseline.
- batch=1, cache=prefix-aggressive, max_tokens=512, candidate-v1: pass-rate 81%, p90 1.05s, cost 0.74x baseline but higher hallucination on entity-update subset.

Notes on reproducibility:
- Runbook available: github link (see linked artifacts). Please use the provided run config (s3://redwood-experiments/throughput-ladder/sep2025) which includes seed lists and container images. All cells use the same seed schedule for deterministic sampling.

Open questions for design reviews:
- What is acceptable long-form quality delta for premium customers? (Product)
- Should we prefer longer canaries for quantized candidates by default? (SRE + Product)
- How to automate selection of cache aggressiveness per-route based on prompt fractiles? (Runtime + Applied-ML)

If you want raw tables or the full run CSVs dropped into Drive, ping me and I'll export the full artifacts.

-- Ava
